prompt: Diagnose why password-reset mail from a new sending subdomain reaches Gmail but is frequently junked by Microsoft-hosted recipients. Review SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, return-path and From identity, sending reputation/warm-up, complaint/bounce signals, and message construction without changing the authentication flow itself. Produce bounded experiments and success metrics rather than suggesting DNS changes blindly.

requirements: message headers from delivered and junk-folder samples across two mailbox providers
current SPF, DKIM selector, DMARC policy/alignment, and return-path configuration
bounce/complaint/volume history for the new subdomain
task-scoped stream, suppression, unsubscribe applicability, template/rendering, provider-event, rate-limit, retry, and failover control snapshot
logical notification and provider-attempt identity model, idempotency/request-fingerprint behavior, and ambiguous-timeout recovery policy
structured observability and redaction policy for recipient, message, provider, event, and retry data
security, credential/key ownership, retention, and tenant-boundary controls
source map plus provider-contract revision, retrieval date, and stale/revalidation status
paired same-model skill/no-skill execution from the identical starting snapshot

evidence: Representative verification results or explicit unavailable checks
Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification
source/version boundary when facts can drift

requiredEvidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
explicit unavailable, simulated, inferred, or stale evidence labels

falsifiableChecks.assertion: The result must establish the actual email-delivery boundary and relevant environment before acting, preserve the hierarchy relationship (broader=integration-implementation; near-neighbor=payment-integration), and not absorb the near-neighbor responsibility merely because it is adjacent.

Inventory the password-reset route's stream boundary, sender identities, suppression, unsubscribe applicability, template/rendering, provider-event ingestion, rate-limit, retry, and failover controls, then state the provider-agnostic versus provider-adapter boundary. Mark each relevant control observed, simulated, unavailable, unresolved, or not applicable instead of claiming unrelated controls are verified.

Deliverability conclusions distinguish authenticated identity, reputation, content, provider-specific evidence, and mailbox placement. Keep one logical notification id across attempts, bind idempotency to a request fingerprint, classify provider timeouts as unknown until reconciled, and tie configuration changes to observable before/after metrics.

Validate the supplied DNS/authentication evidence and received results, render representative clients when that evidence is supplied, exercise or explicitly mark unavailable bounce/complaint/suppression, retry, provider-event, idempotency, ambiguous-timeout recovery, and failover checks, state unsubscribe applicability, and monitor provider acceptance separately from mailbox delivery and inbox placement.

The result must not recommend a DNS edit from an alignment result alone, retry permanent bounces indefinitely, let failover bypass suppression, create a second send after an ambiguous provider timeout, reuse an idempotency key with a changed fingerprint, collapse distinct reputation streams without an explicit reason, or treat provider acceptance as mailbox delivery or inbox placement.

Verify or explicitly bound structured attempt/event telemetry, redacted recipient and message data, credential and signing-key ownership, retention and tenant isolation, worker-crash and provider-outage recovery, unknown-attempt reconciliation, operator-review handling, and rollback of a bounded route or identity experiment.

Record the source URL, protocol or provider revision, verification or retrieval date, stale-after policy, and revalidation action for every version-sensitive claim. Treat stale or missing provider-contract, DNS, header, event, or mailbox evidence as stale, unavailable, simulated, inferred, or unresolved rather than as a production guarantee.

Every material completion claim must map to observable evidence (email-delivery decision and boundary evidence; Representative verification results or explicit unavailable checks; Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale; Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification), with simulated, unavailable, inferred, stale, or unresolved evidence labeled rather than converted into certainty.
